https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/i-h.title: I Had a Clinical Presumption. I Built Tools to Examine It.
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/i-h.description: A question about glucose monitoring became an evidence review, two presentations, and a lesson in why clinical responsibility includes the interface.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/end.description: AI agents are making implementation cheaper. In healthtech, the advantage moves to clinicians who can preserve clinical truth and supervise the architecture.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/oma.title: Omarchy for Physician-Developers: Build a Linux Development Lab
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/oma.description: A beginner-friendly guide to turning a spare computer into a focused Omarchy workstation for Git, containers, AI coding agents, and small clinical software projects.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ana.title: The Anatomy of a Medical AI Hallucination
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ana.description: Medical AI hallucinations become dangerous when plausible invention enters a clinical workflow. A physician-developer's guide to grounding, verification, harnesses, and human accountability.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.title: Physicians Need to Learn the Harness, Not Just the Model
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.description: DeepSeek Harness shows why physicians must understand the context, tools, permissions, logs, and human checkpoints that turn an AI model into a working system.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Ambient Scribe Is Disappearing
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: Ambient clinical AI is moving beyond note generation into an encounter layer that prepares orders, prescriptions, coding, and follow-up while keeping consequential decisions visible to the physician.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/med.title: Medical Education Does Not Need an AI Course. It Needs a New Clinical Curriculum.
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/med.description: Preparing physicians for agentic AI requires more than an elective. Medical education must redesign how students reason independently, delegate work, verify machine output, and retain clinical judgment.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.title: The Physician Above the Loop: Preparing Medicine for Agentic AI
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.description: Clinical intelligence is becoming abundant. Physicians must learn to delegate, verify, contextualize, and judge the work of increasingly autonomous clinical AI systems.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/i-s.title: I Switched Password Managers at 35,000 Feet
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/i-s.description: A difficult login over airplane Wi-Fi forced me to act on research I had already done: leave NordPass, move to 1Password, and stay loyal to the workflow rather than the vendor.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/why.title: Why I Rebuilt Doctors Who Code
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/why.description: Doctors Who Code began as a blog encouraging physicians to learn programming. It is now a learning platform for physicians who want to use AI with judgment and build clinical tools that improve care.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Optimization Trap: What With Folded Hands Can Teach Us About AI in Medicine
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: Jack Williamson's 1947 story imagined machines that obeyed humanity perfectly and destroyed it anyway. Medicine is building the same objective function.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ign.title: Medicine's Crisis Is Not Ignorance. It Is Ineptitude.
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ign.description: Atul Gawande's framework for human failure explains why obstetric emergencies are lost to execution, not knowledge. The fix is a systems problem, not a training problem.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/git.title: GitHub Gists: The Most Underrated Tool Every Physician-Developer Should Be Using
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/git.description: GitHub Gists look like scratch space for code snippets. Used correctly, they become a version-controlled clinical reference library that decks, apps, and blog posts can all cite from a single source.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/fda.title: FDA Clearance Is Not a Monitoring Plan
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/fda.description: Clinical AI can fail without crashing. Physician-developers must build the monitoring, outcome linkage, and human checkpoints that keep cleared software safe after deployment.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/fro.title: From Meetings to Modules: Redefining Clinical Coordination
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/fro.description: Clinical teams do not move slowly because clinicians are slow. They move slowly because pages, meetings, and verbal handoffs force physicians to keep re-explaining decisions that software should carry forward.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/sur.title: Surviving the AI-Native Transformation: A Physician-Developer's Guide
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/sur.description: AI makes clinical software cheap to produce. It does not make it safe. Physician-developers must build systems in which speed remains subordinate to evidence, judgment, and the doctor-patient relationship.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/wee.title: Weekend Project: Sending Emails to My Second Brain
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/wee.description: I built a pipeline that turns any email into a tagged Markdown note in my Obsidian vault, using nothing but Gmail, Apps Script, and the GitHub API.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ai-.title: AI's Next Breakthrough Is Not a Bigger Brain. It Is a Memory You Can Trust.
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ai-.description: The AI race has been about model size for years. The real bottleneck is memory: trustworthy, auditable knowledge that persists across years, not conversations. Medicine will feel this shift first.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/pat.title: Patient Data Liberation Is Not Patient Data Protection
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/pat.description: Wearables connected to medical records are not just a patient-access story. They are a boundary-design problem for doctors who code.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/why.title: Why Your Clinic Workstation Needs a GPU
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/why.description: A clinic workstation with local GPU inference changes the privacy, latency, and ownership posture of clinical AI workflows.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Rare Condition You Have Seen Ten Times
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: Why a physician's second brain turns scattered rare cases into a queryable clinical registry owned by the clinician who lived them.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/lar.title: Clinical AI Should Help Us Find the Growth Restriction Cases We Miss
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/lar.description: Fetal growth restriction is not just an ultrasound diagnosis. It is a longitudinal data problem. Clinical AI will not replace MFM judgment, but it can help surface the pregnancies whose risk is already visible in the record.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Lemonade Machine Problem
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: Automation in medicine should not be judged against an ideal clinician. It should be judged against real human variance, machine variance, supervision, and the cost of failure.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/cli.title: The Moment a Clinical Tool Becomes Infrastructure
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/cli.description: A short introduction to a DoctorsWhoCode series on spreadsheets, tests, and retrieval as the basic discipline of physician-built clinical software.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/fro.title: From Excel to Python: When Your Spreadsheet Becomes a Liability
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/fro.description: Excel is often the right first move for a physician-builder. The problem begins when clinical logic stays trapped in a container that can no longer safely hold it.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/why.title: Why Your Clinical Calculator Needs Tests
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/why.description: A clinical calculator is not safer because it is written in code. It becomes safer when its expected behavior is explicit, checked, and protected from silent drift.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/rag.title: RAG Is the Bridge Between Medical Knowledge and Medical Practice
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/rag.description: Clinical AI earns workflow trust only when its answers are grounded in current, local, auditable knowledge. Retrieval is not a feature. It is infrastructure.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/you.title: You Are Still Prompting. You Should Be Building Agents.
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/you.description: Prompting has a ceiling. Once you hit it, you are coordinating every step manually while the AI handles individual tasks. Here is the framework and three live workflows I use to cross that line.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/bur.title: Burnout Is Not From Working Too Hard. It Is From Working on the Wrong Things.
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/bur.description: For physician-developers, burnout often comes from low-value technical friction. The answer is not more endurance. It is better delegation to systems, automation, and agents.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/han.title: Hantavirus at Sea: What the MV Hondius Outbreak Teaches Physician-Developers
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/han.description: The MV Hondius outbreak was not only a rare infectious disease story. It exposed familiar failures in travel history, triage logic, outbreak data exchange, and emergency logistics.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ai-.title: I Gave an AI Agent 94 Skills and Let It Help Run My Clinical, Coding, and Theology Workflows
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ai-.description: Three weeks into running Hermes Agent in production, I can say this: the real value is not the model. It is the workflow ecosystem wrapped around it. Here is what 94 specialized skills looks like in a real physician-developer stack.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/her.title: The Architecture Behind My 24/7 AI Operations Partner
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/her.description: The model is not the product. The workflow is the product. Here is a technical look at the production stack behind a physician-built AI operations partner: Docker, Traefik, model failover, rate limits, logs, HIPAA boundaries, and the failure modes I watch for every week.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/dea.title: Dead Weight: What a 1970 Cardiology Textbook Taught Me About the Future of Clinical Evidence
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/dea.description: A half-century-old textbook on congenital heart disease. A chapter on Ebstein's anomaly. A comparison that changed how I think about evidence, AI, and what we owe the next generation of physicians.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Jetsons Problem in Clinical Medicine
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: Artificial intelligence in clinical medicine promises abundance. The real risk is not too little data, but too little agency, attention, and equity.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Last Step Is Not Software. It Is Judgment.
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: Clinical software can execute protocol logic perfectly and still be wrong for the patient. The physician checkpoint must remain part of the architecture.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ste.title: Steve Ballmer and the Hard Truth About Healthcare Code
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ste.description: Steve Ballmer's enterprise playbook explains why brilliant clinical software dies in procurement. Part I of The Architects, a series on the software leaders physician-developers must study.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Middle Path, Part I: Doomers, Dismissers, and the Physician Between Them
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: Assess AI claims through evidence, system design, and accountability. The first lesson in The Middle Path, with a clinical case and self-assessment.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/bui.title: Build the Clinical Engine Before the Interface
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/bui.description: A reliable clinical application separates guideline logic from presentation, tests expected behavior, and carries provenance into every recommendation.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/del.title: Delivery Date AI and the Meaning of a Due Date
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/del.description: What ultrasound-based delivery prediction means for clinical care, and how physician-developers can preserve its meaning in the medical record.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/mak.title: Make the Clinical Logic Visible Before You Code
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/mak.description: Translate a clinical protocol into explicit inputs, branches, thresholds, exceptions, and failure states before choosing a programming language.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/you.title: Your First Agentic Workflow: Delegate a Small, Verifiable Project
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/you.description: A physician-developer's practical guide to giving an AI agent one bounded software assignment and requiring a plan, tests, review evidence, and a stopping condition.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/a-p.title: A Protocol Is a Memory System, Not a Patient
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/a-p.description: Clinical protocols reduce avoidable variation, but software must preserve their population boundaries, exceptions, provenance, and judgment points.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Harness Is the Workplace: Choosing Where an AI Agent Works
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, OpenClaw, Hermes, and Omarchy illustrate a durable lesson for physicians: choose the agent's workplace before delegating the work.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/fro.title: From Chatbot to Agent: The Mental Model Every Physician Needs
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/fro.description: AI agents do more than answer questions. This physician-developer guide explains the agent loop, levels of autonomy, and the checkpoints that keep humans accountable.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/evi.title: Evidence Is Not Yet a Clinical Instruction
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/evi.description: Clinical evidence describes populations. Physician-developers must preserve its limits before translating it into protocol logic or software.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/bui.title: Build the Minimum Viable Clinical Harness
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/bui.description: A clinical AI workflow needs more than a model and a prompt. Build the smallest system that can scope, retrieve, generate, verify, challenge, approve, execute, and audit the work.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/sam.title: Same Model, Different System
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/sam.description: Claude Code, Google Antigravity, OpenAI Codex, and DeepSeek Harness expose the architecture around an AI model. Physicians should compare that architecture before comparing model rankings.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Prompt Is a Clinical Specification
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: Clinical prompting is not a contest for better wording. It is the work of defining sources, context, objectives, prohibitions, and evaluation before a model generates anything.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The One-Week Ambient Challenge
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: A seven-day self-audit for physicians using an approved ambient documentation system, built around three questions that matter more than words per minute.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/bui.title: Build an Ambient Documentation Lab Before You Buy One
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/bui.description: You can learn the entire ambient documentation pipeline with a phone, a fictional patient, and a general-purpose AI assistant, before spending a dollar on a clinical platform.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/you.title: Your First Ambient Note Is Not Your Final Workflow
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/you.description: Most physicians stop optimizing an ambient documentation system the moment it produces a usable note. That is the moment the real work should start.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/tea.title: Teach the Tech, Not the Vendor
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/tea.description: Ambient documentation vendors will change, merge, and disappear. A ten-point evaluation framework that outlasts any single product.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ai-.title: AI Drafts. The Clinician Verifies. That Line Cannot Move.
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ai-.description: Speech recognition misses words. Language models infer things that were never said. A disciplined review habit is what separates ambient AI from a liability.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/amb.title: Ambient AI Let Me Stop Interrupting My Patients
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/amb.description: When documentation time is scarce, physicians steer patients toward answers that are easy to type. Ambient AI removes the excuse for doing that.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Three-Phase Ambient Workflow Every Physician Should Build
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: Pre-encounter, encounter, and post-encounter are not just note sections. They are the three places an ambient workflow can quietly go wrong.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/amb.title: Ambient Documentation Is Not Transcription
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/amb.description: A transcript and a clinical note are not the same object. Understanding the pipeline between them is the difference between using ambient AI and trusting it blindly.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/nur.title: Nurse Benjamin's Warning: Thirty Years of Clinical Documentation
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/nur.description: From paper charts at Harlem Hospital in 1992 to ambient AI in 2026, the tools changed four times. The physician's responsibility toward the record did not.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/doc.title: Ambient Documentation Was Never About Speed
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/doc.description: Ambient clinical AI is usually sold as a time-saver. The real change it offers is different: it can give the physician's attention back to the patient.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/flu.title: Fluent Answers Are Not Clinical Judgment
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/flu.description: Language models can make uncertain medical information sound finished. The problem is not fluency. The problem is mistaking fluency for accountable clinical reasoning.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/jou.title: Journals Are Becoming Infrastructure
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/jou.description: Medical journals are no longer only read by clinicians. They are becoming upstream inputs to AI systems. That makes provenance, evidence hierarchy, and distribution part of clinical infrastructure.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Search Box Is Disappearing
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: Medicine is moving from retrieval to synthesis. That changes the physician's work from finding information to judging synthesized information under clinical pressure.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/fat.title: Fatigue, Failure, and the Data That Brought Me Back
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/fat.description: After six weeks of missed training, my PGIS morning check-in revealed what a GPS watch alone never shows: glycemic and autonomic recovery run on entirely different clocks.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/bui.title: Building the Physician's Knowledge Flywheel
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/bui.description: Why the vault gets exponentially more valuable the more you use it. The long-game thesis: this is the clinical infrastructure that vendors cannot build.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/my-.title: My Slides Became Code: Why I Use Marp for AI-Generated Presentations
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/my-.description: Marp lets physician-builders turn reviewed knowledge into version-controlled, AI-assisted teaching decks without surrendering clinical responsibility.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ai-.title: AI Agents Do Not Replace Software Fundamentals. They Expose Whether You Have Any.
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ai-.description: For physician-builders, agentic engineering is not prompt magic. It is bounded context, vertical slices, observability, and accountability.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Thinking Partner Commands Every Physician Should Build
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: Slash commands that replace the morning literature review. /challenge, /emerge, /connect, /close-clinic, /graduate: clinical reasoning augmentation, not automation.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/cod.title: Codex on Mobile Solves the Async Doctor Problem
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/cod.description: OpenAI bringing Codex into the ChatGPT mobile app is not about coding on a phone. It is about supervising agentic work when your clinical day refuses to give you uninterrupted time.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Physician's Stack: Obsidian + Claude Code + Local LLM
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: How to build a clinical knowledge vault without sending patient data to anyone's server. The two-vaults architecture, ingestion workflows, and the HIPAA-first policy.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/wha.title: What Karpathy Actually Built (and Why It Matters for Medicine)
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/wha.description: The compilation analogy, explained for clinicians. How LLM Wiki compiles clinical knowledge into synthesized entity pages instead of re-retrieving chunks on every query.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Physician's Second Brain: A 5-Post Series
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: A complete guide to building an LLM-powered clinical knowledge vault. Why existing PKM failed physicians, how to build one that works, and why this is the infrastructure layer physicians must own.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The PKM System That Was Never Built for You
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: Why every personal knowledge management app failed physicians specifically, and why Karpathy's April 2026 LLM Wiki changes everything.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Map Has Blind Spots
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: Move 37 was not a parlor trick. It was a warning. Physician-developers need to be ready for the moment AI starts finding medically important patterns our inherited maps never taught us to see.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ai-.title: AI Just Outperformed Physicians at Clinical Writing. This Should Not Surprise You.
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/ai-.description: HealthBench Professional shows AI has already crossed the threshold in clinical writing and documentation. The real lesson is not replacement. It is that physician-developers need to build the harness.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/whe.title: When AI Told a Dying Man What He Wanted to Hear
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/whe.description: Joe Riley trusted AI over his oncologist and died of a treatable cancer. His tragedy wasn't naivety — it was earned distrust, amplified by a machine that had no way to know the difference.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The PDF Wall: Why Your Clinical RAG Keeps Hallucinating
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: Your clinical RAG system is not hallucinating because the model is bad. It is hallucinating because your document pipeline is broken. Here is what clinical PDF parsing actually requires, and why Docling is the fix.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.title: Deployment: When Your Code Becomes Clinical Reality
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.description: An app on your laptop helps no one. Deployment is the step where physician-developer work finally becomes available to patients, colleagues, and clinics.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.title: Postgres and Prisma: Where the Data Actually Lives
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.description: Clinical software becomes real when it remembers. This is the database layer that turns a one-off calculator into a longitudinal tool.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.title: Tailwind CSS: Design Without Asking a Designer
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.description: Patients do not trust ugly calculators. Tailwind helps physician-developers build interfaces that feel clean, credible, and ready to use.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.title: Astro: Building Fast, Clinical-Grade Websites Without the Bloat
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.description: Physician-developer projects are usually content-first. Astro fits that shape by shipping less JavaScript, faster pages, and cleaner performance by default.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.title: MDX: Where Writing Meets Code
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.description: Most physician writing dies in static documents. MDX turns clinical education into living pages that can explain, calculate, and update in one file.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.title: AI-Assisted Coding: Your Second Pair of Hands
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.description: Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot do not replace judgment. They compress the feedback loop for physician-developers who still read every line before they ship.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.title: Python: The Language of Clinical Data
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.description: JavaScript runs in the browser. Python runs behind the workflow, where lab values, CSV exports, data cleaning, and clinical models actually live.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.title: TypeScript: Because a Misplaced Decimal Can Hurt a Patient
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.description: Clinical software cannot afford vague inputs. TypeScript gives physician-developers safer contracts, clearer data shapes, and fewer silent failures.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.title: JavaScript: The Language Your Patients Already Run
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.description: Every patient portal, tablet consent form, and browser-based clinical tool already runs JavaScript. This is where physician-developers start changing what medicine feels like on a screen.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.title: The Physician-Developer's Stack: Nine Tools. One Doctor. A Workflow That Actually Ships.
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/phy.description: A practical 10-part Doctors Who Code series for physicians who want to build and ship clinical tools with the modern web stack, from JavaScript to deployment.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/dee.title: Deep Work for Physicians: Protecting the Cognitive Core of Medicine
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/dee.description: Deep work is not a productivity hack for doctors. It is a clinical safety issue, a training issue, and a systems design issue. Physicians need to protect deep thinking and automate the shallows.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.title: The Human Bottleneck: Why Medicine's Agentic Future Is Waiting on Us
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/the.description: AI agents are 50x faster than humans, but medicine only captures a fraction of that speed. The real bottleneck in agentic AI is not the technology — it is human capacity, clinical oversight, and workflows built for the wrong consumer. A physician-developer's perspective.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/loc.title: The Local Advantage: Why Physician-Developers Should Build on Local LLMs Instead of Consumer AI
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/loc.description: Consumer AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude are useful. But a physician-developer who deploys a locally fine-tuned model on controlled infrastructure has something more powerful: a clinical tool that learns your practice, respects your data, and costs less at scale.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/cli.title: Clinical Documentation Automation Should Remove Friction, Not Replace the Doctor
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/cli.description: Documentation automation is not a typing solution. It is a workflow design problem. For physicians and physician-developers, the real goal is protecting clinical judgment from administrative drag.

https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/i-b.title: I Built PGIS Recipes Because Food Systems Need Architecture
https://www.doctorswhocode.blog/blog/i-b.description: PGIS Recipes started as a stack of Marp slide decks. I turned it into a GitHub Pages library because nutrition guidance only compounds when the delivery system is structured, durable, and easy to revisit.
